Complete Empirical Research Plan

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Two–stage least-squares (instrumental-variables) panel regression with checker and very‐high-frequency time fixed effects.

Rationale  
• The outcome (own items-per-second) and the regressor of interest (average contemporaneous productivity of co-workers on duty) are jointly determined – the standard “reflection problem.”  
• Cashiers’ shift assignments are set bi-weekly by a queuing rule based on seniority rather than ability, and within-day overlaps start/stop at pre-set clock times. Thus the presence of particular peers is plausibly exogenous to demand shocks within the 10-minute interval.  
• We can construct an instrument that is (i) predetermined and (ii) varies only with the shift roster, not with moment-to-moment demand: the roster-weighted mean of co-workers’ historical (pre-sample) productivity, i.e. “ex-ante peer ability.”  
• Fixed effects absorb all checker-invariant factors and time-varying factors common to every worker in the store (e.g., demand spikes, promotions, holidays).

Supplementary strategy (mechanism test): Difference-in-differences comparing the IV coefficient for peers who are mutually visible versus peers who are in the store but not in the focal cashier’s line of sight.  A larger effect for the visible set identifies social pressure/monitoring rather than pure demand spillovers.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (continuous)  
PEER_PROD_it  =  mean(items scanned/second) of all OTHER cashiers j≠i working in store s during 10-minute interval t.

Instrument  
PRED_PEER_ABILITY_it =  mean(𝛽̂_j) of co-workers on duty, where 𝛽̂_j is cashier j’s average productivity in a totally separate estimation sample (e.g. the first six months of data or leave-one-shift-out).  

Control group / counterfactual  
Intervals in which the same cashier works with lower-ability peers provide the counterfactual; individual fixed effects guarantee the comparison is within worker.

Treatment timing  
Varies every 10 minutes as co-workers arrive/depart.

(For the DID mechanism check define VIS_PEER_PROD_it using only registers that face the focal cashier and NONVIS_PEER_PROD_it for the rest.)

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------
IV-specific  
A1 Relevance: Roster-weighted peer ability predicts actual peer productivity in the interval.  
Plausible: Ability is persistent and roster composition is the main determinant of mean peer speed.

A2 Exclusion: Given high-frequency store-time fixed effects, roster-weighted peer ability affects worker i’s speed only through contemporaneous peer productivity, not through unobserved demand, managerial pressure, or shift characteristics.  
Plausible because (i) wages are fixed, (ii) managers do not target high-ability workers to busy periods, and (iii) any remaining store-time demand shock is absorbed by the 10-minute store*clock-time FE.

A3 Independence: Peer ability is as good as random conditional on the fixed effects – i.e. the seniority-based assignment rule does not systematically pair particular workers.  
Plausible; seniority determines only which preferred shifts are granted, not the identity of the other cashiers on duty.

Panel FE model  
A4 SUTVA: One cashier’s outcome depends only on co-workers in the same store at that moment, not on distant stores or future peers.  Reasonable given geographic separation.

DID mechanism test  
A5 Parallel peer‐type trends: In the absence of visibility the coefficients on visible vs. non-visible peers would be the same.  With symmetric registers and no selective schedule by visibility, this is plausible.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Remedies
-------------------------------------------------
T1 Endogenous sorting of high-ability workers into high-demand intervals  
Remedy: 10-minute STORE × DATE × CLOCKTIME fixed effects + IV using ex-ante ability break the link between contemporaneous demand and the instrument.

T2 Simultaneity / reflection (own productivity contained in peer average)  
Remedy: Use leave-i-out mean for the endogenous regressor; instrument with roster-weighted ability so the first-stage is predetermined.

T3 Measurement error / customer mix (basket size heterogeneity)  
Remedy: Control flexibly for mean basket size in the interval, the coefficient of variation of basket size, and number of open registers.  Also show robustness using inverse-hyperbolic-sine of items/second which attenuates outliers.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------
```r
#------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load packages
#------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast manipulations
library(fixest)       # fast high-dimensional FE & IV
library(readr)

#------------------------------------------------
# 2. Read data
#------------------------------------------------
d <- fread("supermarket_scanner_data.csv")  # each row is checker × 10-min

#------------------------------------------------
# 3. Variable construction
#------------------------------------------------
# items per second
d[, prod := items_scanned / seconds]

# Identify shift_id (e.g., store-day-checker shift)
d[, shift_id := rleid(checker_id, store_id, date)]

# Historical (pre-sample) ability: use first 6 months
d[, sample_half := ifelse(date < "2004-01-01", "pre", "post")]
ability <- d[sample_half == "pre", .(ability = mean(prod, na.rm = TRUE)),
             by = checker_id]

# Merge back
d <- merge(d, ability, by = "checker_id", all.x = TRUE)

# For each 10-minute interval build peer variables
setkey(d, store_id, datetime)
# Helper: list of workers per interval
d[, n_other := .N - 1, by = .(store_id, datetime)]
d[, peer_prod := (sum(prod) - prod)/n_other, by = .(store_id, datetime)]
d[, peer_ability := (sum(ability) - ability)/n_other, by = .(store_id, datetime)]

# Visible vs. non-visible (requires register map)
# Assume binary variable 'visible_to_i' already supplied for every dyad;
# pre-aggregate outside this snippet or omit for brevity.

#------------------------------------------------
# 4. Main 2SLS specification
#   own_prod = beta * peer_prod   (endogenous)
#           + FE(worker) + FE(store*datetime) + error
# Instrument: peer_ability
#------------------------------------------------
est_main <- feols(prod ~ 1 | checker_id + store_id^datetime | 
                    peer_prod ~ peer_ability,
                  data = d, vcov = "cluster_checker_id")
summary(est_main)

#------------------------------------------------
# 5. Mechanism DID: visible vs non-visible
#------------------------------------------------
# Assuming we created vis_peer_prod and nonvis_peer_prod and their ability counterparts
est_vis <- feols(prod ~ 1 | checker_id + store_id^datetime | 
                   vis_peer_prod + nonvis_peer_prod ~ vis_peer_ability + nonvis_peer_ability,
                 data = d, vcov = "cluster_checker_id")
summary(est_vis)

#------------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness: leave-one-week-out ability
#------------------------------------------------
ability_loo <- d[, .(ability_loo = mean(prod, na.rm = TRUE)), 
                 by = .(checker_id, week = week(date))]
# merge shifted left out week-by-week (not shown in detail)

# Re-run regression with alternative instrument
#------------------------------------------------
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------
Prior: Positive social spillovers outweigh free riding in this setting because (i) effort is observable to nearby peers, and (ii) slow cashiers impose a very visible external cost (longer lines).  My best guess is an elasticity in the range 0.1–0.2: a 10 percent increase in mean peer productivity raises own productivity by roughly 1–2 percent.

For the mechanism test I expect the IV coefficient on VIS_PEER_PROD to be at least twice as large as that on NONVIS_PEER_PROD, consistent with monitoring or contagious enthusiasm.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
-------------------------------------------------
C1 Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10) ............ 1  
C2 Exclusion restriction plausibility .................. 0.8  
C3 Random/ignorable assignment of peer ability ......... 0.8  
C4 SUTVA / stable interference structure ............... 0.9  
C5 No differential measurement error ................... 0.9  

Overall: While no single assumption is guaranteed, the combination of high-frequency store*time fixed effects, predetermined instrument, and institutional scheduling rules make the design credible.
